title: Frequency Data and SNP Analysis
subtitle: SNPs in populations, disease association and the limits of SNP testing
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: collect, record and present data to represent frequencies of characteristics in a population, in order to identify trends, patterns, relationships and limitations in data, for example: examining frequency data, analysing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
Conduct a secondary-source investigation on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in populations and their association with a genetic disease
Assess potential limitations and constraints of SNP testing and databases in diagnostic medicine
inquiryQuestion: Can population genetic patterns be predicted with any accuracy?
lessonIntent: Students can explain what a SNP is, calculate and compare allele frequencies in a case and control sample, explain what a SNP and disease association does and does not show, and assess the limits of SNP testing and databases in diagnosis.
examSkill: Calculate allele frequencies from genotype counts, compare groups with cautious frequency language, then qualify the conclusion with a limitation of SNP testing or the database.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Biology. Today, SNPs, frequency data and what a genetic test can really tell you. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: One letter, one disease
scenes.body: Sickle cell disease comes from a single base change in the haemoglobin gene: an A replaced by a T.
scenes.callout: If one letter can cause a disease, can one letter predict your health?
scenes.caption: Sickle cell disease is caused by one base substitution in the beta globin gene, a single nucleotide difference.

voiceover.text: Alright, here's a remarkable fact. Sickle cell disease, which affects millions of people worldwide, comes down to a single letter in the DNA. In the gene for the beta chain of haemoglobin, one A has been replaced by a T. That swaps one amino acid in the protein, and it's enough to make red blood cells collapse into a sickle shape when oxygen is low. A single base difference like that, found at a particular position in the genome, is called a single nucleotide polymorphism, or SNP. Your genome contains millions of them. So here's the question for today. If one letter can cause a disease, can reading a handful of letters predict your health? We'll look at what SNPs are, how scientists link them to disease using frequency data, and why a SNP test result needs to be read very carefully.

scenes.heading: SNPs: one base, many comparisons
scenes.body: A SNP is a position in the genome where individuals differ by a single base.

bullets.text: At a SNP position, one person might carry an A where another carries a G.
Millions of SNPs are scattered through the genome, mostly in noncoding DNA.
Each version is an allele, so SNPs have frequencies in a population.

scenes.secondary: Most SNPs have no effect at all. A few change a protein or its regulation, and some sit close to a gene that does.
scenes.callout: A SNP is one letter that varies between people.
scenes.caption: SNPs are common single base differences; each version is an allele with a population frequency.

voiceover.text: So what exactly is a SNP? It's a single position in the genome where people differ by one base. At that spot, one person might carry an A, while another carries a G. SNPs are everywhere, there are millions of them scattered through the genome, and most sit in noncoding DNA where they make no difference at all. A few land inside a gene and change the protein, like the sickle cell SNP, and some sit close to a gene and affect how strongly it's expressed. Here's the part that links to frequency data. Each version of a SNP is an allele, so just like any other allele, it has a frequency in a population. That means we can count it, compare it between groups, and look for patterns, and that's exactly how SNPs get linked to disease.

scenes.heading: Linking a SNP to a disease
scenes.body: Scientists compare how common a SNP allele is in people with a disease and in people without it.

bullets.text: Cases: a sample of people who have the disease.
Controls: a similar sample of people who don't.
An allele much more common in cases is associated with the disease.

scenes.secondary: Studies that scan hundreds of thousands of SNPs at once like this are called genome wide association studies.
scenes.callout: Association means 'found together more often', not 'causes'.
scenes.caption: Case and control comparisons reveal SNP alleles associated with a disease.

voiceover.text: Now, how do scientists actually link a SNP to a disease? The classic design compares two groups. The cases are a sample of people who have the disease, and the controls are a similar sample of people who don't. Researchers read the same SNP positions in everyone, then calculate how common each allele is in each group. If one allele turns up much more often in the cases than the controls, that allele is said to be associated with the disease. Scale that up to hundreds of thousands of SNPs across thousands of people, and you've got a genome wide association study. But hold onto that word, associated. It means the allele and the disease are found together more often than chance would suggest. It doesn't, on its own, mean the SNP causes the disease.

scenes.heading: Case versus control frequency
scenes.question: A study genotypes 500 people with a disease and 500 without it at one SNP. Cases carry 300 copies of the T allele; controls carry 150. Calculate the T allele frequency in each group, compare them, and give one limitation.
scenes.coachNote: Each person has two copies of every autosomal SNP, so 500 people carry 1000 alleles.
steps: Total alleles in each group: 500 people × 2 = 1000 alleles.
In this sample the T allele is twice as common in cases as in controls, so it is associated with the disease.
Limitation: association is not causation; T may simply sit near the real causal variant, and results may not apply to other ancestries.
scenes.caption: T allele: 30% in cases, 15% in controls; associated with disease, but association is not causation.

voiceover.text: Let's work through a data question. A study genotypes five hundred people with a disease and five hundred without it, at one SNP. The cases carry three hundred copies of the T allele, and the controls carry one hundred and fifty. Find the T allele frequency in each group, compare them, and give a limitation. Here's the trap to avoid first. Every person has two copies of each autosomal SNP, so five hundred people carry a thousand alleles, not five hundred. For the cases, three hundred out of a thousand is zero point three, or thirty percent. For the controls, one hundred and fifty out of a thousand is fifteen percent. Now compare, with careful language. In this sample, the T allele is twice as common in cases as in controls, so it's associated with the disease. And the limitation, association isn't causation. The T allele might simply sit near the real causal variant, and the result may not hold in people of a different ancestry.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: SNP: a single nucleotide polymorphism, a one base difference at a genome position.
Allele frequency: copies of one allele divided by all alleles at that position.
Association: an allele found with a disease more often than chance predicts.
SNP test: reading a chosen set of SNP positions, often on a DNA chip.
Genetic database: a stored collection of sequences or variants used for comparison.

scenes.callout: Allele frequency counts alleles, not people.
scenes.caption: SNP, allele frequency, association, SNP test, genetic database.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the words. A SNP, a single nucleotide polymorphism, is a one base difference at a particular position in the genome. Allele frequency is the number of copies of one allele, divided by all the alleles at that position in the sample, so remember you're counting alleles, not people. Association means an allele is found together with a disease more often than chance would predict. A SNP test reads a chosen set of SNP positions in a person's DNA, often using a DNA chip that checks hundreds of thousands of positions at once. And a genetic database is a stored collection of sequences or variants, used to compare a person's result against what's already known. Those last two are where the limits of testing live, so let's look at them.

scenes.heading: The limits of SNP testing
scenes.body: A SNP test only reads the positions it was designed to read, and interprets them against databases with gaps.

bullets.text: It reads selected positions, so a negative result doesn't rule a disease out.
Most associated SNPs raise risk only slightly; environment and other genes matter.
Databases mostly hold data from people of European ancestry, so accuracy varies.
Rare variants are the ones chips misread most, and some variants have uncertain meaning.

scenes.secondary: For example, some consumer tests check only three BRCA variants, while more than a thousand harmful BRCA variants are known.
scenes.callout: A SNP test reads a sample of the genome, not the whole story.
scenes.caption: SNP tests read chosen positions, most effects are small, databases are skewed, and rare variants are error prone.

voiceover.text: This is where the newer syllabus wants you to assess, so let's be precise about the limits. First, a SNP test only reads the positions it was designed to read. Some consumer tests check just three variants in the BRCA genes, while more than a thousand harmful BRCA variants are known, so a clear result doesn't rule out risk at all. Second, most disease associated SNPs raise risk only slightly, because common diseases also depend on many other genes and on the environment. Third, the databases used to interpret results are built mostly from people of European ancestry, so predictions tend to be less accurate for everyone else. And fourth, chips are least reliable for exactly the rare variants that matter most, and plenty of variants have no known meaning yet. They're called variants of uncertain significance. So a SNP test reads a sample of the genome, not the whole story.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: 'The allele is more common in patients, so it causes the disease.' Association shows the allele and disease occur together, not that one causes the other.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: 'My SNP test was negative, so I'm not at risk.' The test only checked selected positions against incomplete databases. A negative result lowers uncertainty for those variants only.
scenes.callout: Associated is not causal, and negative is not all clear.
scenes.caption: Association is not causation; a negative SNP test only covers the variants it read.

voiceover.text: Two traps to avoid. Trap one, reading an association as a cause. A student sees that an allele is more common in patients and writes that it causes the disease. That's an overclaim. The allele might sit right next to the real causal variant and simply be inherited along with it, or the two groups might differ in ancestry. To show cause, you need extra evidence, like finding the variant changes how a protein works. Trap two is about individual results. Someone gets a negative SNP test and concludes they're not at risk. But the test only checked selected positions, against databases that are incomplete. A negative result tells you about those particular variants, and nothing about the ones that weren't read. So associated isn't causal, and negative isn't an all clear.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A SNP associated with type 2 diabetes was found in a study of 20,000 people of European ancestry. A clinic in Australia plans to use it alone to diagnose diabetes risk in all its patients. Give two limitations.
answerSteps: One SNP captures only a small part of risk; type 2 diabetes depends on many genes plus diet and exercise.
The association came from one ancestry group, so it may be weaker or absent in patients of other ancestries.
The SNP may only be a marker near the real causal variant, not the cause itself.
Answer: a single, possibly non causal SNP from one ancestry group can't reliably diagnose risk for everyone.
scenes.caption: One SNP from one ancestry group cannot diagnose a complex disease's risk for a whole clinic.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A SNP associated with type 2 diabetes was found in a study of twenty thousand people of European ancestry. A clinic in Australia plans to use that SNP alone to diagnose diabetes risk in all its patients. Give two limitations. Pause and find two limitations. OK, there are three strong ones, and you only need two. First, a single SNP captures only a small slice of the risk, because type 2 diabetes depends on many genes, plus diet, exercise and body weight. Second, the association was found in one ancestry group, and an Australian clinic sees patients of many ancestries, so the link may be weaker, or even absent, for some of them. Third, the SNP might only be a marker sitting near the real causal variant, rather than the cause itself. So one possibly non causal SNP, from one ancestry group, can't reliably diagnose risk for everyone.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: A SNP is a single base difference; each version is an allele with a frequency.
Allele frequency = copies of the allele ÷ total alleles (2 per person).
An allele more common in cases than controls is associated with the disease, not proven causal.
SNP tests read selected positions, so a negative result is not an all clear.
Databases are skewed toward European ancestry, and rare variants are misread most.
scenes.finalPrompt: SNP data question? Calculate the frequencies, compare them with cautious language, then name a limitation of the test or the database.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: SNPs, allele frequency, association, test limits, database limits.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, a SNP is a single base difference in the genome, and each version is an allele with its own frequency in a population. Second, allele frequency is the copies of that allele divided by the total alleles, and remember there are two per person. Third, when an allele is more common in cases than in controls, it's associated with the disease, but that alone doesn't prove it's the cause. Fourth, SNP tests only read selected positions, so a negative result is never an all clear. And fifth, the databases behind the tests are skewed toward people of European ancestry, and rare variants are the ones most often misread. So on any SNP data question, calculate the frequencies, compare them with cautious language, then name a limitation of the test or the database.
